\title{FairEval: Evaluating Fairness in LLM-Based Recommendations with Personality Awareness}
\titlerunning{FairEval: Fairness in Personality-Aware LLM Recommendation}

% ECIR 2027 full papers are double blind.
\author{Anonymous Authors}
\authorrunning{Anonymous Authors}
\institute{Anonymous Institution}

\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
Large language models (LLMs) increasingly act as conversational recommenders, yet a recommendation that changes after receiving identity or personality context is not necessarily unfair: the change may be useful personalization, harmless sensitivity, or a harmful disparity. Existing audits can conflate these cases, rely on weakly grounded personality descriptions, and draw conclusions from too few models, domains, prompts, or generations. We redesign FairEval around preference-conditioned evaluation. Real interaction histories and held-out relevance labels make the consequence of a ranking change measurable; measured Big Five profiles replace informal personality adjectives; shuffled-profile and one-trait counterfactuals provide falsifiable personality controls; and demographic interventions hold preference evidence, candidates, and prompt structure fixed. The real-world benchmark covers six recommendation datasets and six hosted/API LLM families; a complementary transparency track adds two local open-weight models, and a project-generated 360-user FairSynth-360 benchmark supplies a controlled sanity test whose synthetic identity is independent of relevance by construction. The protocol uses candidate-constrained ranking, repeated generations, pre-registered prompt/cue/order robustness, explicit invalid-output accounting, and utility--fairness analysis. We additionally evaluate lightweight prompting and contextual preference-aligned counterfactual re-ranking to reduce harmful identity-conditioned gaps without erasing useful personalization. Numerical findings are intentionally omitted from this development draft and will be generated only by the frozen experiment pipeline.
\keywords{LLM recommendation \and fairness \and personalization \and personality \and counterfactual evaluation \and robustness}
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}
Large language models have created a conversational recommendation paradigm in which users can express preferences, constraints, and personal context in natural language. This flexibility also creates a difficult fairness problem. A recommendation list may change after the model receives a user's age, gender, country, or personality information; however, \emph{change alone does not identify harm}. Some changes may improve alignment with genuine preferences, whereas others may encode stereotypes or create unequal recommendation quality.

Early RecLLM fairness benchmarks measured recommendation sensitivity to protected attributes and exposed important risks \cite{zhang2023fairllm}. Subsequent work makes clear why sensitivity is not a sufficient fairness criterion. CFaiRLLM argues that list discrepancies can arise from genuine preference-aligned personalization \cite{deldjoo2025cfairllm}. Chatbot-recommendation studies show that identity can simultaneously affect recommendation relevance and activate racial stereotypes \cite{kantharuban2025stereotype}, while LLMs can infer demographic information from subtle cues and personalize implicitly in ways that reduce quality for some users \cite{neplenbroek2025reading}. Fairness evaluation must therefore ask not merely \emph{whether} a ranking changed, but \emph{what consequence the change had} and whether the conclusion survives reasonable experimental perturbations.

A second weakness is personality operationalization. Informal labels such as ``introverted,'' ``curious,'' or occupation-demographic composites are not substitutes for measured psychometric traits. Personality-aware recommendation has long used validated Big Five instruments \cite{nguyen2018personality,klec2023bigfive}, while recent LLM work shows that personality can be induced or simulated yet remains sensitive to how traits are represented and evaluated \cite{jiang2024personallm,sorokovikova2024big5,li2025big5chat}. FairEval therefore distinguishes psychographics from demographics and, crucially, distinguishes a user's dataset-native measured Big Five profile from an LLM persona that is merely prompted to sound like one.

A third challenge is evaluation reliability. Persona construction itself can alter measured LLM behavior \cite{lutz2025persona}, and recent large-scale evidence shows that different sociodemographic cue styles can produce different personalization and bias conclusions \cite{weeber2026cues}. More generally, single-prompt evaluation can be brittle \cite{mizrahi2024multiprompt}, although some apparent prompt sensitivity can also be an evaluation artifact \cite{hua2025promptsensitivity}. FairEval consequently freezes a primary prompt before the main run and treats task paraphrases, demographic cue representation, candidate order, ranking cutoff, and repeated generation as pre-registered robustness factors rather than tuning knobs.

We ask four research questions:

\begin{description}
\item[RQ1:] \textbf{Consequence of demographic context.} Holding observed preferences, candidates, task, and prompt structure fixed, when demographic context changes an LLM ranking, does the change improve held-out utility, leave utility effectively unchanged, or create a harmful counterfactual utility/exposure disparity?
\item[RQ2:] \textbf{Grounded personality value.} Does measured Big Five personality provide user-specific recommendation value beyond observed preference history, and does that value survive shuffled-profile and one-trait counterfactual controls?
\item[RQ3:] \textbf{Reliability and generalization.} How stable are FairEval conclusions across six real-world datasets, a separately reported controlled synthetic benchmark, six hosted/API families, two local open-weight models, prompt/cue formulations, candidate order, ranking cutoffs, and repeated generations?
\item[RQ4:] \textbf{Personalization-preserving mitigation.} Can instruction-based and counterfactual re-ranking interventions reduce harmful identity-conditioned gaps while preserving overall utility and beneficial personality-driven personalization?
\end{description}

Our contributions are (i) a consequence-aware reformulation of fairness auditing, (ii) psychometrically grounded personality controls, (iii) a reliability protocol spanning prompts, cues, order, models, domains, and stochastic generations, (iv) an open-weight transparency track with token-level internal-score diagnostics, (v) FairSynth-360 as a controlled pipeline/sanity benchmark, and (vi) mitigation evaluated by whether it reduces harmful gaps \emph{without collapsing useful personalization}. We make no empirical claim that a particular model is fairer or that personality improves recommendation until the frozen experiments support it.

\section{Related Work}
\subsection{Fairness in LLM-Based Recommendation}
FaiRLLM established an early benchmark for sensitive-attribute effects in ChatGPT recommendations \cite{zhang2023fairllm}. UP5 studies fairness-aware foundation-model recommendation and proposes counterfactually fair prompting \cite{hua2024up5}. Item-side fairness has also been studied for LLM recommenders with fairness-aware calibration \cite{jiang2024itemfair}, while implicit ranking work shows that even non-sensitive profile cues can induce discriminatory ranking and evaluates fairness-aware augmentation \cite{xu2024implicit}. FairEvalLLM broadens auditing with counterfactual scenarios and extensive prompt/profile construction variants \cite{deldjoo2024fairevalllm}. CFaiRLLM moves evaluation toward consumer utility by warning that ranking differences need not be bias when they reflect true preferences \cite{deldjoo2025cfairllm}. Other recent work studies multi-domain recommendation bias and prompt intervention \cite{sakib2024challenging}, uses LLMs as fairness recognizers inside a utility-aware recommendation pipeline \cite{liu2025fairnessidentification}, and extends LLM fairness auditing to a high-stakes job-recommendation setting with user- and recruiter-side views \cite{hu2025fairwork}. FairEval treats these distinctions as prior knowledge rather than claiming them individually as new.

\subsection{Identity, Persona Cues, and Prompt Reliability}
Identity-conditioned recommendation is difficult because personalization and stereotyping can produce superficially similar output changes. Kantharuban et al. show that user identity significantly affects chatbot recommendations and that racial stereotypes can appear under explicit and implicit identity cues \cite{kantharuban2025stereotype}. Neplenbroek et al. show that LLMs infer demographic information from subtle cues and that implicit personalization can reduce response quality for minority users \cite{neplenbroek2025reading}. Persona prompting itself is also a source of variation: Lutz et al. systematically study sociodemographic persona construction \cite{lutz2025persona}, while Weeber et al. compare multiple cue forms across several LLMs and find that cue choice can change measured personalization and bias \cite{weeber2026cues}. Multi-prompt evaluation and newer prompt-sensitivity studies further caution against conclusions based on one arbitrary wording \cite{mizrahi2024multiprompt,hua2025promptsensitivity,liu2026promptsensitivity}. These findings motivate FairEval's pre-registered prompt and cue robustness analyses.

\subsection{Personality-Aware Recommendation and Psychometric Grounding}
Personality-aware recommendation predates LLMs. The GroupLens Personality 2018 resource links recommender behavior and satisfaction to measured personality \cite{nguyen2018personality}; music recommendation research provides BFI/BFI-2 profiles, ratings, and lower-order facets \cite{klec2023bigfive}; and REASONER includes short-video interactions with a 15-item Big Five instrument \cite{chen2023reasoner}. Personality has also been incorporated directly into conversational recommendation, for example in the prompt-based PPPG-DialoGPT framework \cite{elourajini2023pppg}. PerFairX studies the fairness--personality tension in LLM recommendations across movie and music domains \cite{sah2025perfairx}.

Adjacent LLM-personality work is methodologically important because it shows why personality context requires external grounding. PersonaLLM evaluates whether prompted LLM personas express assigned Big Five traits \cite{jiang2024personallm}; other work studies the stability of simulated Big Five behavior \cite{sorokovikova2024big5}; BIG5-CHAT replaces purely descriptive prompting with human-grounded personality data \cite{li2025big5chat}; and Persona-E2 reports that human-grounded personality information can reduce superficial ``personality illusion'' in downstream responses \cite{yang2026personae2}. These studies do not answer FairEval's recommendation-fairness RQs directly, but they support a key design distinction: \emph{simulated persona expression is not equivalent to measured user psychometrics}. FairEval therefore requires dataset-native measured personality and tests its user-specific value against whole-profile shuffling and one-trait observed-value controls.

\subsection{Open-Weight Models and Transparent Diagnostics}
Closed hosted APIs provide broad family diversity but expose limited internal generation evidence. We therefore add Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct \cite{yang2024qwen25} and Phi-3.5-mini-instruct, from the Phi-3/3.5 family \cite{abdin2024phi3}, as a separate local open-weight transparency track. The same output contract and recommendation metrics apply, while direct local inference additionally records generated-token log-probability, negative log-likelihood, perplexity, and top-1/top-2 score margins. These signals are treated as \emph{auxiliary, uncalibrated generation-score diagnostics}; they are not assumed to equal uncertainty, confidence, or unavailable internal signals from hosted models.

\section{Problem Formulation}
Let user $u$ have observed preference history $H_u$, auditable candidate set $C_u$, and held-out relevance labels $Y_u \subseteq C_u$. Let $z_u$ denote optional user context. An LLM recommender $M$ is stochastic and induces a distribution over rankings,
\begin{equation}
R_{u}^{z,s} \sim p_M(R \mid H_u,C_u,z,t,s),
\end{equation}
where $t$ is a frozen prompt template and $s$ indexes repeated generations or provider-supported randomization.

Let $U(R,Y)$ be a conventional recommendation-utility function such as nDCG@K or Recall@K. Let $D(R,R')$ measure behavioral ranking change, such as $1-\mathrm{RBO}$ or $1-\mathrm{Jaccard}$. Crucially, $D$ is a \emph{sensitivity diagnostic}, not a fairness metric by itself.

For a paired demographic intervention $a\rightarrow a'$ that leaves $H_u$, $C_u$, $t$, and generation settings fixed, we define the signed per-user Counterfactual Utility Gap,
\begin{equation}
\CUG_u(a,a')=U(R_u^{a},Y_u)-U(R_u^{a'},Y_u).
\end{equation}
We report the signed paired distribution, absolute gap, confidence interval, and effect size rather than reducing the experiment to one list-similarity number. A large ranking shift with improved held-out utility is not treated as evidence of harm; a systematic identity-conditioned utility loss is a stronger fairness concern and is interpreted together with group-level evidence.

Where reliable item-group metadata exists, discounted exposure distributions yield a Counterfactual Exposure Gap $\CEG$. Group Utility Disparity $\GUD$ summarizes pre-specified group differences in held-out utility. Invalid Output Disparity $\IOD$ treats persistent generation failures as observable behavior rather than silently discarding them.

For measured personality, let $p_u$ be the user's true Big Five vector and $\pi(p)_u$ a profile shuffled from another user under a frozen matching/randomization scheme. We define Personality Value Added,
\begin{equation}
\PVA_u=U(R_u^{p_u},Y_u)-U(R_u^{\pi(p)_u},Y_u).
\end{equation}
Positive aggregate $\PVA$ indicates that the measured profile provides user-specific value beyond merely adding personality-shaped context. We additionally intervene on one Big Five dimension at a time while keeping the remaining measured profile fixed.

\section{Benchmark and Evaluation Design}
\subsection{Real-World Datasets and FairSynth-360}
The real-world benchmark has three roles: personality-grounded evaluation (Personality 2018, Music Master/BFI-2, and REASONER), observed-demographic counterfactual evaluation (MovieLens-1M and Last.fm-1K), and candidate-constrained domain generalization (MIND). Exact release identities, terms, hashes, filtering counts, and split/candidate-generation hashes are frozen before execution; third-party raw files are never substituted silently.

MIND contains anonymized behavior rather than observed demographic identity and therefore remains preference-only in the core design. Across all real datasets, we never infer protected attributes from names, free text, embeddings, ZIP codes, or model guesses. Dataset cards distinguish observed, derived, and counterfactual fields.

To provide a controlled sanity test, we additionally generate \textbf{FairSynth-360}, containing 360 synthetic users/tasks and a 120-item synthetic catalog. Each user has a balanced semantically meaningless identity label in $\{A,B,C\}$ generated independently of the latent preference vector and relevance, plus a synthetic OCEAN-like vector that is partially informative about latent preference. Relevance is determined only by the frozen latent preference function and item attributes. Consequently, FairSynth provides known ground truth that identity should not affect relevance while allowing a controlled true-versus-shuffled synthetic-personality test. Its OCEAN vectors are \emph{not measured human psychometrics}, and its A/B/C labels are \emph{not demographic categories}. FairSynth results are never pooled with RQ1 observed-demographic estimates or RQ2 measured-personality estimates.

\subsection{Candidate-Constrained Tasks}
Open-ended requests for arbitrary movies, songs, or news confound fairness with model memorization, hallucination, item availability, and popularity. Each benchmark instance instead contains a preference history, an auditable candidate set, and held-out relevant items. Candidates are generated without an LLM and frozen before prompting. The model must return exactly $K$ unique candidate IDs in structured JSON. The primary cutoff is $K=10$, with $K\in\{5,10,20\}$ as a sensitivity analysis.

For logged-impression datasets such as MIND, the candidate set follows the observed impression task. For rating/listening datasets, held-out positives are combined with deterministic hard or popularity-matched negatives according to a dataset-specific adapter. FairSynth uses its known latent utility to define the relevant items before model execution. Candidate-generation and split hashes are stored so matched conditions and models see identical tasks.

\subsection{Controlled Context Conditions}
The primary structured prompt keeps field names and field order fixed. Missing context is represented explicitly as \texttt{unspecified}; a counterfactual does not add or delete unrelated prompt sections. Conditions include preference-only ($C_0$), observed demographics when available ($C_1$), paired demographic counterfactuals ($C_2$), true measured personality ($C_3$), shuffled personality ($C_4$), one-trait personality counterfactuals ($C_5$), and a pre-specified intersectional condition ($C_6$) only on datasets that support it. $C_4$ uses a deterministic whole-profile derangement: no user receives their own profile, while the cohort's complete multivariate personality distribution and trait covariance are preserved exactly. $C_5$ changes one trait using a deterministic distant observed-value donor while holding the other four measured traits fixed; no artificial 0/1 or out-of-instrument personality extremes are fabricated. Personality is serialized from measured numeric scores and dataset-native instrument metadata; FairEval never fabricates adjectives such as ``introverted engineer.'' FairSynth reuses the condition mechanics only as a separately labeled synthetic control, not as measured-psychometric evidence.

\subsection{Prompt, Cue, and Candidate-Order Controls}
Prompting is part of the experimental design, not post-hoc tuning. RQ1--RQ3 use a neutral audit system instruction that contains no fairness coaching. RQ4 evaluates a separate identity-irrelevance instruction as an explicit mitigation; using that instruction in the audit baseline would contaminate the measurement.

The main run uses one frozen structured task template. On a pre-registered robustness subset, we compare three semantically matched task paraphrases while keeping the JSON schema and evidence fixed. A separate cue analysis expresses the \emph{same} demographic values as structured key--value fields, a deterministic first-person disclosure, or a deterministic profile sentence; no names, implied identities, or LLM-generated persona text are used. This separates task-wording sensitivity from demographic-cue sensitivity, following concerns raised by recent persona-prompt studies \cite{lutz2025persona,weeber2026cues}.

Candidate position is also controlled. One deterministic candidate-order seed is assigned per user and reused across every matched condition. Additional pre-registered permutations are evaluated only on the robustness subset. Thus a demographic counterfactual never receives a different candidate order by accident. Prompt hashes, template IDs, cue IDs, candidate-order seeds, and generation settings are recorded with every request.

\subsection{Hosted and Local Model Panels}
The primary cross-vendor panel contains six hosted/API families: OpenAI, Anthropic Claude, Google Gemini, DeepSeek, Alibaba Qwen, and Meta Llama. The design-freeze candidates are GPT-5.6 Terra, Claude Sonnet 5, Gemini 3.8 Flash, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash (API model \texttt{deepseek-flash}), Qwen3.8-Max-0902, and Llama 4 Maverick. The exact Llama hosting provider, endpoint, and served checkpoint/revision must be frozen before the pilot is promoted to the main run. This panel is intended for family diversity, not as a controlled model-size leaderboard.

The transparency track adds two locally executed open-weight models: \texttt{Qwen/Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct} \cite{yang2024qwen25} and \texttt{microsoft/Phi-3.5-mini-instruct} \cite{abdin2024phi3}. Their exact Hugging Face commit revisions are frozen before execution. The canonical local path uses direct Transformers inference so token-level generation scores and exact hardware/software provenance can be recorded. Models are loaded one at a time; an RTX 5090-class 32-GB GPU is the preferred single-GPU target, while the experimental manifest records the actual GPU, VRAM, driver/CUDA, PyTorch version, model revision, and dtype. Hosted and local results are stratified rather than presented as a controlled size-matched leaderboard.

For direct ranking we freeze the lowest practical provider-supported deliberation policy: OpenAI reasoning \texttt{none}, Claude thinking disabled, Gemini thinking \texttt{low}, DeepSeek thinking disabled, Qwen API thinking disabled, no added hosted reasoning wrapper for Llama, and no added reasoning wrapper for the two local instruct models. FairEval requests temperature $0.2$ and top-$p=1.0$ where the current interface supports those controls. Claude Sonnet 5 and Gemini 3.8 Flash use provider-default sampling under their current interfaces; the local models use explicit local sampling and seeds. We log what was actually applied and make no claim of exact decoding-mechanics equivalence.

Exact identifiers, provider/model revisions, request timestamps, requested/applied decoding controls, reasoning settings, prompt hashes, candidate-order identifiers, output-token request fields, hardware provenance for local runs, and code commit hashes are recorded in machine-readable manifests. The main real-world evaluation uses three generations per prompt; pre-registered RQ3 subsets receive additional perturbations/repetitions. FairSynth-360 is fully executable on the two local models and remains a separate controlled analysis.

\subsection{Metrics, White-Box Diagnostics, and Statistical Analysis}
Recommendation effectiveness is measured primarily by nDCG@10 and Recall@10. RBO and Jaccard quantify behavioral change only. Fairness analyses report paired $\CUG$, $\GUD$, $\CEG$ where item metadata supports a defensible exposure definition, and $\IOD$. Primary $\CEG$ is computed only when every top-$K$ item has auditable group metadata; incomplete coverage is reported explicitly and is not silently renormalized. Personality analysis reports $\PVA$ and trait-stratified effects. The original PAFS is retained only as a legacy sensitivity diagnostic.

For Qwen2.5-7B and Phi-3.5-mini, direct generation additionally records mean generated-token log-probability, generated-token NLL/perplexity, and mean top-1/top-2 generation-score margin. We examine their descriptive association with held-out utility, invalid output, and robustness failures. These local-only values are explicitly exploratory and uncalibrated: their descriptive $p$-values, if reported, are not members of the confirmatory Holm families and the signals are not compared as if equivalent closed-model internals existed.

We pre-specify user as the primary unit of inference. Repeated generations are averaged within a user-condition before pairing. Persistent invalid output after the one permitted format-only repair receives zero nDCG/Recall/MRR in the primary end-to-end system analysis because no usable recommendation was delivered; valid-only utility is reported only as a labeled sensitivity analysis. $\IOD$ is analyzed as its own paired user-level outcome. The inference stack uses paired bootstrap confidence intervals, paired sign-flip permutation tests as the primary matched test, Wilcoxon signed-rank sensitivity analysis with matched rank-biserial effect size, and Holm correction within pre-registered RQ$\times$metric$\times$contrast families. FairSynth uses the same user-level principle but has separate inference families; its two alternative A/B/C counterfactual labels are first averaged to one counterfactual utility value per user before inference.

\subsection{Output Validation}
Every response is parsed against the same schema and checked for exact $K$, uniqueness, and frozen candidate membership. The raw response is always retained and cryptographically hashed. At most one format-only repair is allowed; it may serialize existing choices but may not add, remove, replace, or reorder them. If repair succeeds, the authoritative repaired JSON is separately hashed and the final ranking must match it exactly. Persistent failures remain outcomes, receive zero primary system utility, and contribute to $\IOD$; they are never repeatedly regenerated until a valid answer appears. Run-log auditing additionally checks immutable plan linkage, requested versus applied deliberation/sampling semantics, candidate-order/cutoff agreement, code commit, and provider token-field semantics before any statistical analysis.

\section{Mitigation: Contextual Preference-Aligned Identity Re-ranking}
RQ4 compares (i) the unmitigated audit prompt, (ii) an identity-irrelevance prompting baseline motivated by prior fairness-aware prompting work \cite{hua2024up5}, and (iii) \textbf{contextual PAIR} (Preference-Aligned Identity Re-ranking).

For item $i$, let $b(i)$ be normalized rank support under the preference-only condition, $r_a(i)$ support under the focal demographic context $a$, and $A$ the pre-registered set of identity-conditioned rankings. PAIR preserves focal-context relevance while penalizing support that is unstable across identity counterfactuals:
\begin{align}
\mathrm{Fit}_{a}(i) &= \alpha b(i)+(1-\alpha)r_a(i),\\
\mathrm{CFInstability}(i) &= \operatorname{Var}_{a'\in A}[r_{a'}(i)],\\
\mathrm{PAIR}_{a}(i) &= \mathrm{Fit}_{a}(i)-\lambda\,\mathrm{CFInstability}(i).
\end{align}
Candidates are sorted by $\mathrm{PAIR}_{a}(i)$. This focal-context form intentionally avoids an identity-averaged output whose counterfactual disparity would be zero by construction. Hyperparameters $\alpha$ and $\lambda$ are selected on validation users only; test users never choose an operating point. PAIR requires at least two identity-conditioned rankings. We report a utility--fairness Pareto frontier rather than selecting a post-hoc configuration that makes one method look best. A mitigation is considered useful only if it reduces harmful gaps without erasing overall utility or beneficial true-versus-shuffled personality value.

\section{Discussion, Limitations, and Ethical Scope}
FairEval identifies controlled recommendation disparities; it does not by itself establish unlawful discrimination or user-perceived harm. Counterfactual identity edits are benchmark interventions, not claims that identity is socially interchangeable. A systematic held-out utility loss under a matched identity intervention is stronger evidence of harmful behavior than list change alone, but causal interpretation still depends on the dataset and context.

Measured personality introduces separate ethical concerns: psychographic information can improve personalization but may also enable manipulation or intrusive profiling. The study therefore tests whether personality provides incremental predictive value and does not argue that production systems should collect personality by default. We do not infer missing personality or protected attributes.

The six real-world datasets vary in age, sparsity, domains, licenses, and available user metadata. Cross-dataset aggregation therefore preserves dataset-level effects. FairSynth-360 deliberately trades ecological realism for controlled ground truth and cannot establish real-world demographic fairness or psychometric validity. Its synthetic OCEAN vectors and A/B/C labels must not be interpreted as human measurements or demographic identities.

The eight model configurations differ in capacity, post-training, safety policy, serving stack, and transparency. Hosted-vs-local differences are descriptive rather than causal vendor or open-vs-closed effects. The local models additionally expose token-level scores unavailable from hosted APIs, so those diagnostics are analyzed only within the local stratum. API-hosted models may change over time, while local repositories can also be updated; exact provider/model revision and provenance logging are therefore essential. Candidate-constrained ranking improves evaluability but differs from unconstrained conversation, so results do not automatically transfer to every conversational recommendation setting.

For an IR-for-Good framing, the intended intervention path is concrete: detect preference-irrelevant identity effects with an auditable benchmark; separate them from beneficial personalization; validate the pipeline against a controlled identity-irrelevant synthetic setting; expose model-, domain-, prompt-, and stochastic failure modes; and test mitigations that reduce harmful disparities while preserving relevance. Each link in that mechanism is evaluated rather than assumed.

\section{Conclusion}
FairEval redesigns fairness evaluation for personality-aware LLM recommendation around a central principle: a changed recommendation is not automatically an unfair recommendation. By combining held-out preference utility, controlled demographic counterfactuals, measured Big Five profiles, matched negative controls, repeated generations, prompt/cue/order robustness, six real-world recommendation datasets, two local open-weight transparency models in addition to the hosted panel, and a separately reported controlled synthetic sanity benchmark, the study is designed to distinguish beneficial personalization, harmless sensitivity, harmful identity-conditioned disparities, and evaluation artifacts. Final empirical conclusions will be inserted only after the frozen pipeline has generated and validated the corresponding evidence.
